title: The day it all went wrong
goal: Tell a story in the past: keep the background in the Past Continuous and the events in the Past Simple.
warmup: What is the worst weather you have ever walked home in?
When did you last oversleep? What happened next?
Tell me about a small thing that ruined a whole day.

main.task: Tell the story of a day that went wrong — yours, or invented.
main.howto: Two minutes. Set the scene first (what was going on), then the events one after another. Use at least three linkers and two strong adjectives.
prompts: How did the day start? What were you doing when it went wrong?
What happened first — and then?
How did you feel at that moment? Use a strong adjective, not 'very'.
Was there a moment when it got even worse?
How did it end? Were you relieved, or was it still awful?

phrases: It all started when…
While I was… , suddenly…
By the time I got there…
I was absolutely freezing / starving / exhausted.
Luckily, … / Eventually, …
And then, to make things worse…
followup: Is it funny now, or still annoying?
What would you do differently if the same morning happened tomorrow?
teacher: Let him finish the whole story without corrections, then replay two or three sentences back with the tense fixed — he hears the difference better than he reads it.

title: A day in your life
goal: Talk about your routine in the Present Simple and switch to the Present Continuous when you describe today.
warmup: What time did you wake up today? Was that early or late for you?
What is the first thing you do after you get up?
Are you a morning person or a night person? Why?

main.task: Describe your normal Wednesday, then say how today is different.
main.howto: Speak for about two minutes without stopping. Use at least four time expressions and switch to the Present Continuous when you talk about today.
prompts: Morning: what time, in what order, how long it takes you
School: when it starts, when you have a break, when you get home
Afternoon: homework, hobbies, friends
Evening: dinner, screens, what time you go to bed
And today? What is different from a normal Wednesday?

phrases: I usually… but today I'm…
It takes me about twenty minutes to…
After that I…
On weekdays I… , at the weekend I…
I hardly ever… / I never…
followup: If you could change one thing about your morning, what would it be?
Whose routine in your family is the strangest?
Would you like to start school at 10 a.m.? What would you lose?
teacher: Count out loud how many times the tense switch is correct and say the number at the end — it turns accuracy into a small game.

title: Free time and hobbies
goal: Talk about hobbies with play / go / do and tell a short story about the past.
warmup: What did you do last weekend?
How often do you do your hobby — every day, twice a week, or less?
Which hobby would you never try? Why not?

main.task: Tell the story of how you started your hobby.
main.howto: Two minutes, in the past. Begin with when it started and finish with how it is going now.
prompts: When and how did you start? Who showed you?
What was difficult at the beginning?
Tell one funny or bad moment — what happened?
How often do you do it now?
Would you like to be really good at it, or is it just for fun?

phrases: I took it up when I was…
At first it was hard because…
One day I was… when suddenly…
I'm quite good at… / I'm not very good at…
I'm really into…
followup: Is it better to have one hobby or many?
Do your parents think your hobby is useful?
What hobby do you think you will have at 30?
teacher: If the story dries up after three sentences, ask 'and then what happened?' twice — it usually doubles the length.

title: Getting to know you
goal: Give longer answers about yourself instead of one word.
warmup: Tell me three things about yourself — one of them false. I'll guess which.
Describe your best friend in five sentences.
What are you good at that people don't expect?

main.task: Describe a person in your family without saying who it is.
main.howto: Speak for a minute and a half. I have to guess the person from your description.
prompts: What do they look like?
What do they do every day?
What makes them different from everyone else?
What do you argue about?
What have you learnt from them?

phrases: He / She looks…
The thing about him / her is…
We always argue about…
What I like about them is…
followup: Who in your family are you most like?
Is it easier to describe someone you love or someone you don't?
teacher: Ban one-word answers out loud at the start — 'every answer is at least two sentences' — and hold to it.
